exercises.video_explanation_script: The standing barbell overhead press is the king of shoulder exercises. Start with the bar at your upper chest, hands just outside shoulder-width, elbows slightly forward. From here, press the bar straight up, but here's the key: you need to move your head back slightly to let the bar clear your face. Once the bar passes your forehead, press your head through to a neutral position. Lock out fully at the top with the bar directly over your mid-foot. Lower under control back to your chest. Keep your core tight and glutes squeezed throughout to protect your lower back. This exercise builds powerful, well-developed shoulders.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The seated dumbbell overhead press is excellent for building shoulder size and strength. Set your bench to nearly vertical - about 85 to 90 degrees. Sit with your back firmly against the pad and dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Press the dumbbells up and slightly inward so they nearly touch at the top - don't clang them together. Fully extend your arms at the top. Then lower under control back to shoulder level. The key is keeping your back against the pad throughout the entire movement. This variation allows you to focus purely on the shoulders without worrying about lower back stability.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Lateral raises are the best exercise for building wide shoulders. Stand with a slight forward lean, dumbbells at your sides, and a slight bend in your elbows. From here, raise the dumbbells out to your sides, leading with your elbows like you're elbowing someone. At the top, your arms should be parallel to the floor - that's shoulder height. Here's a key detail: rotate your wrists slightly so your pinkies are a bit higher than your thumbs, like you're pouring water from a pitcher. This internal rotation maximizes lateral deltoid activation. Lower under control and repeat. Use lighter weight than you think you need and focus on feeling your side delts working.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Cable lateral raises offer a huge advantage over dumbbells - constant tension throughout the entire range of motion. Set the cable pulley to the lowest position and stand perpendicular to the machine. Reach across your body with the hand furthest from the machine and grab the handle. From here, raise the cable out to your side, leading with your elbow, until your arm is parallel to the floor. The cable creates resistance the entire way, unlike dumbbells where tension drops off at the top. Control it back down, resisting the pull of the cable. You should feel constant tension in your side delt throughout every rep. This makes cables excellent for building that mind-muscle connection and achieving a great pump.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Front raises directly target the front of your shoulders. Stand with dumbbells in front of your thighs, palms facing your legs or facing each other. With a slight bend in your elbows, raise the dumbbells straight out in front of you until they reach eye level or just above shoulder height. Keep your shoulders packed down - don't shrug them up. Control the weight back down to your thighs. The key is eliminating momentum and using strict form. Your front delts already get a lot of work from pressing movements, so you don't need to go heavy here. Focus on the squeeze and control.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Face pulls are one of the most important exercises for shoulder health and development. Set a cable pulley to upper chest height with a rope attachment. Stand facing the machine and grab the rope with an overhand grip. From here, pull the rope toward your face while simultaneously separating the rope ends. Your elbows should go high and out to the sides - think about making a double bicep pose. At the end, your hands should be by your ears, the rope should be split apart, and your thumbs should be pointing behind you. Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard. This exercise builds your rear delts, improves posture, and keeps your shoulders healthy. Everyone should be doing face pulls.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The reverse pec deck is one of the best machines for isolating your rear delts. Adjust the seat so the handles are at shoulder height, then sit facing the pad with your chest pressed firmly against it. Grab the handles and from here, pull them back by leading with your elbows. Think about trying to touch your elbows together behind your back. At the end, squeeze your shoulder blades together hard. Control the weight back to the starting position and feel that stretch in your rear delts. The machine makes it really easy to focus on the mind-muscle connection without worrying about balance or stabilization. This is an essential exercise for balanced shoulder development.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Bent-over rear delt flies are excellent for targeting those often-neglected rear deltoids. You can do these standing bent over or seated leaning forward - either way, your torso should be close to parallel with the floor. Let the dumbbells hang straight down with a slight bend in your elbows. From here, raise the dumbbells out to your sides, leading with your elbows. Lift until your arms are parallel to the floor and squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control and repeat. The key is maintaining a flat back throughout - if your back is rounding, the weight is too heavy or you need to work on your hip hinge. This exercise is crucial for balanced shoulder development and healthy shoulders.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The Arnold Press, named after Arnold Schwarzenegger, is an advanced shoulder exercise that hits all three heads of the deltoid. Start seated or standing with dumbbells at shoulder height, but here's the twist: your palms are facing toward you, not away. Press the dumbbells up while simultaneously rotating your palms outward. At the top, your palms should be facing forward just like a regular press. Lower back down while reversing the rotation, ending with palms facing you again. The rotation is what makes this special - it hits your front delts at the bottom, transitions to your side delts during the rotation, and emphasizes your front and side delts at the top. This is an advanced movement, so use lighter weight than you would for a standard press and focus on smooth, controlled rotation.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Cable upright rows are great for building shoulder width and trap development. Set a cable pulley to the lowest position with a bar or rope attachment. Stand facing the machine and hold the attachment at arm's length. From here, pull the attachment straight up your body, leading with your elbows. Your elbows should rise up and out, going higher than your hands. Pull until your elbows are at least at shoulder height - that's where you get maximum shoulder activation. Control it back down and repeat. The key is leading with your elbows, not your hands. Some people experience shoulder discomfort with this exercise - if that's you, try using a rope attachment or a wider grip, or simply skip this exercise. There are plenty of other great shoulder exercises.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The landmine press is one of the most shoulder-friendly pressing exercises you can do. Anchor a barbell in a landmine attachment or securely in a corner. Hold the end of the bar at your shoulder and stand in a staggered stance for stability. From here, press the bar up and forward in a natural arc motion until your arm is fully extended. The arc path is what makes this so shoulder-friendly - it's a more natural pressing angle that reduces the risk of shoulder impingement. Lower under control back to your shoulder. Keep your core braced throughout to prevent your lower back from arching. This is an excellent exercise for building shoulder strength and size, especially if traditional overhead pressing bothers your shoulders.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Single-arm dumbbell presses are excellent for building shoulder strength while challenging your core stability. Stand or sit with one dumbbell at shoulder height. Here's what makes this special: as you press the dumbbell overhead, your core has to work incredibly hard to prevent your torso from leaning or rotating. Press straight up to full extension while keeping your hips square and your torso upright. It's harder than it sounds - that unilateral load wants to pull you off center. Lower under control and repeat. This exercise builds not just strong shoulders, but a rock-solid core and exposes any strength imbalances between sides. Use lighter weight than you would for a bilateral press and focus on that core stability.
